source.title: SAMSON: Sharpness-Aware Minimization Scaled by Outlier Normalization for Improving DNN Generalization and Robustness
source.authors: Gonçalo Mordido; Sébastien Henwood; S. Chandar; Franccois Leduc-Primeau

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study trains and evaluates sharpness-aware methods on natural image labels, reporting test accuracy and a sharpness measure. It does not test the claim versions’ specified train–test gap, optimizer comparisons, or memorization conditions.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy for several methods and models, and separately relates sharpness to robustness under simulated weight noise. It does not report random-label memorization, train error, or the train–test generalization gap. The robustness gap is between clean and noisy inference, so it is not the gap in V7.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization premise to develop SAMSON and evaluates method performance and hardware-noise robustness. None of its results tests V1–V8. In particular, its sharpness correlations concern clean-to-noisy test-accuracy loss, not the training–test generalization gap required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main conclusion but overstates uniform superiority. The authors conclude that SAMSON improves noiseless performance across tested architectures and training regimes, that combining it with aggressive weight clipping improves weight-noise robustness, and that its sharpness measure correlates strongly with robustness within training configurations. The best SAMSON variant depends on architecture and dataset, and ASAM slightly outperforms both variants on DenseNet-40/CIFAR-10.
record.recipe_differences: The method modifies sharpness-aware training by scaling perturbations using weight magnitude and layer weight range; it compares SAMSON with SGD, SAM and ASAM. It evaluates standard test accuracy, not memorization of random labels or the train–test gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Best SAMSON variant depends on dataset and architecture; ImageNet finetuning uses selected neighborhood sizes; robustness comparisons use noise level and optional clipping or additive noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharpness-aware methods are compared on natural-image test accuracy. The best SAMSON variant has the highest mean accuracy in nine of ten CIFAR architecture–dataset settings; ASAM leads by 0.03 percentage points on DenseNet-40/CIFAR-10. SAMSON also has slightly higher ImageNet finetuning accuracy than SAM and ASAM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAMSON can improve natural-image held-out accuracy relative to the tested training methods, with the best variant depending on architecture and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 6–7 and Appendix C relate sharpness to test-accuracy degradation under noisy weights. The authors report strong within-configuration correlations and improved robustness from SAMSON, particularly with aggressive weight clipping. These are robustness gaps between clean and noisy inference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Magnitude- and range-aware sharpness can correlate with hardware-noise robustness within training configurations, and sharpness-aware training combined with clipping can improve that robustness.

record.problems: The paper reports means and standard deviations over three runs for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 test accuracy, but does not report train accuracy or train–test gaps. ImageNet table values have no uncertainty. Robustness correlations are mainly shown in figures and concern clean-to-noisy inference performance rather than the train–test gap.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit is filled by the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet test-accuracy tables. Robustness results and sharpness-versus-robustness figures in Sections 6–7 and Appendix A–C are omitted; those measure inference degradation under weight noise, not the train–test generalization gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, its coexistence with natural-label generalization, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove large-batch penalties.
Dropout comparisons and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.

Association of magnitude-aware sharpness with training–test gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Magnitude-aware sharpness is measured here, but its empirical correlation target is inference robustness.
Memorization-based example removal versus random removal and resulting test-accuracy changes.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 numerical values match Tables 1–3. Their states remain cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; these are method-performance rows, not claim-effect measurements. Robustness results are already declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries. The record's statement that magnitude-aware sharpness is not tested should be narrowed: it is measured, but not against the generalization gap named in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label test accuracy.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adam or other adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the stated tuning conditions.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
The measured sharpness is related to clean-to-noisy inference accuracy loss, not the train–test generalization gap; magnitude-aware sharpness is not tested.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
